fullPassage: In today's information age, in many companies and on many teams, the weights of individual capabilities and contributions have shifted. The knowledge used to do many jobs is now less private, harder to keep secret. Whereas in the past, authority derived naturally from mastery of information, today many people have access to the same sources. If knowledge is still power, it is a kind of power that is more widely shared. Consistent and repeatable processes and outputs are important, but they are not sufficient to stay competitive. Consistency and repeatability are more likely to suppress fresh thinking than to encourage it. In this knowledge economy, people who are merely managers — people who are primarily monitors of others' work — are of less value to a company than those who think of new ways to do things.

If knowledge is still power, it is a kind of power that is more widely shared. Consistent and repeatable processes and outputs are important, but they are not sufficient to stay competitive. Consistency and repeatability are more likely to suppress fresh thinking than to encourage it. In this knowledge economy, people who are merely managers — people who are primarily monitors of others' work — are of less value to a company than those who think of new ways to do things.
